nature-econ-456.title: Linear programming: planning with straight-line rules
nature-econ-456.text: A farmer with limited land, {{ref:nature-eco-662}} and {{ref:nature-hist-084}} must choose how many hectares of wheat and barley to plant for the most revenue. Linear programming finds the best outcome, such as maximum profit or lowest cost, when the goal and all the requirements are linear relationships, with no curves. It is a special case of {{ref:nature-econ-423}}. The inequalities cut out the set of allowed choices, a many-sided shape called a convex polytope. Leonid Kantorovich and Wassily Leontief independently explored its practical uses in the late 1930s. Kantorovich later shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with T. C. Koopmans. George B. Dantzig developed the general formulation in 1946–1947 for US Air Force planning and invented the {{ref:nature-econ-457}} in 1947. The method shaped early microeconomics and helped inspire key ideas in optimization, such as {{ref:nature-econ-438}} and the importance of convexity. The earliest precursor of the DICE climate-economy model built by {{ref:nature-hist-050}} was a linear programming model of energy supply and demand from 1977.

nature-econ-459.title: Markov decision processes: choosing step by step under chance
nature-econ-459.text: Many decisions repeat under uncertainty: each result is partly luck, and each shapes the next choice. A Markov decision process (MDP) is a {{ref:nature-eecon-240}} of such a sequence. It is defined by states, actions, the probabilities of moving between states, and rewards ({{ref:nature-econ-417}}). The goal is a policy, a rule giving the action for each state, that maximizes the {{ref:nature-econ-756}} of the discounted sum of rewards. MDPs arose in operations research in the 1950s. They are now used in {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, economics, healthcare and reinforcement learning, a branch of machine learning. They are often solved with stochastic, or chance-driven, dynamic programming, where the {{ref:nature-econ-416}} gives the recursion for expected rewards. Exact solutions are often infeasible, because problem size grows exponentially with the number of state and action variables. In game-theory terms, an MDP is a stochastic game with only one player.

nature-econ-479.title: Where growth comes from
nature-econ-479.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-256}} estimated that technological progress accounted for 80 percent of the long-term rise in US income per person, and more capital investment for only 20 percent. Output per person can be broken into four parts. They are output per hour of labour, hours worked, the share of working-age people in work, and the share of people who are of working age. Capital helps, but only up to a point. More capital per worker raises output, yet it faces diminishing returns, partly because of the growing burden of depreciation. Many analyses give a major role to human capital, though it is hard to measure because it is built at home, at school and on the job. It helps growth only if the population is healthy and well nourished. History adds other forces. Moving workers from low-productivity farming to high-productivity manufacturing raised overall output, and laws protecting contracts and private property helped economies move toward capitalism.

nature-econ-517.title: Consumption of fixed capital: the cost of wear in national accounts
nature-econ-517.text: A large cost hides inside every GDP figure. The UN manual says this cost, consumption of fixed capital, may account for 10 per cent or more of total GDP. It is the national-accounts term for depreciation: the fall in the current value of fixed assets over a period through wear, normal obsolescence and normal accidental damage. It is valued at current market prices rather than historic cost, which is why the System of National Accounts avoids the word depreciation. Subtracting it from GDP gives {{ref:nature-acct-119}}, and subtracting it from {{ref:nature-econ-530}} gives {{ref:nature-econ-571}}. That net figure shows the income actually available for consumption and new investment, which makes it a better gauge of economic welfare than GDP. Some losses are left out. It excludes the using up or degradation of non-produced assets such as land, mineral deposits, coal, oil and natural gas. It also excludes assets destroyed by war or rare major natural disasters. Critics note that its economic valuation yields figures that differ from standard accounting practice.

nature-econ-527.title: The Gini coefficient: inequality in a single number
nature-econ-527.text: Corrado Gini published his measure in 1912, building on the work of Max Lorenz. The Gini coefficient sums up how unequally income, wealth or consumption is spread across a nation or group, from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for perfect inequality. It is usually defined from the {{ref:nature-econ-873}}, which plots the share of total income earned by the bottom share of the population. On that chart, a straight 45-degree line means perfect equality. The simplest case shows the logic. With just two income groups, if the high earners are a share u of people and earn a share f of income, the Gini is f − u. It can be calculated on market income, before taxes and transfers, or on disposable income. UNICEF put the net income Gini of Latin America and the Caribbean at 48.3 in 2008, the highest of any region. Ecologists borrow it too, measuring biodiversity by plotting the cumulative share of species against the cumulative share of individuals.

nature-econ-560.title: Monetary policy: steering the economy through interest rates
nature-econ-560.text: When a central bank changes interest rates, the effects ripple outward. Investment, consumption, asset prices and currency values shift, and with them demand, employment and inflation. Economists call this chain the monetary transmission mechanism. Monetary policy is what a nation's monetary authority uses to influence money and financial conditions, in pursuit of goals such as high employment and low, stable inflation. Setting interest rates, directly or through {{ref:nature-econ-563}}, is generally its main tool. Expansionary policy lowers rates to stimulate activity, and contractionary policy dampens activity and inflation. Most developed-country central banks target inflation, while most in developing countries target a fixed value for their currency. Unlike fiscal policy, monetary policy works through financial channels, and it is usually run by central banks independent of government. When rates are near zero, conventional policy cannot loosen further, so central banks may turn to {{ref:nature-econ-564}}.

nature-econ-606.title: The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused
nature-econ-606.text: In 1833 the English economist Lloyd described herders sharing a common grazing field. Each could add extra cattle, and together the extra cattle could lead to {{ref:nature-eco-761}}. The tragedy of the commons is the idea behind that scene. When people share a resource that benefits each user at a cost to everyone, each has a reason to overuse it, so together they use it up. The name comes from a 1968 essay in the journal Science by the ecologist Hardin, who took his title from Lloyd's pamphlet. Hardin's main worry was that there would be too many people, and he wrote that 'freedom in a commons brings ruin to all'. The idea now serves as a model for many resource problems, including water, forests, fish, and oil, gas and coal. Climate change has been described as a huge example, with the Earth treated as a commons depleted without regard to the harm done to others. Proposed government fixes include {{ref:nature-res-266}}, {{ref:nature-val-107}} such as permits for fishing or logging, and making users pay for the harm they cause. Whether the tragedy is inevitable is disputed. Ostrom and colleagues found it less common and easier to solve than Hardin claimed, because local users often design their own rules. Farmers have run one Swiss Alpine commons since 1517. Critics add that historical English common land always had a legal owner, and only people with legal rights, called commoners, could use it.

nature-econ-610.title: Common-pool resources: shared, scarce and hard to fence
nature-econ-610.text: Each fisher on a shared ground has a reason to catch as many fish as possible before someone else does. Soon the stock runs down. Fishing grounds are a common-pool resource: a natural or human-made system that is costly, but not impossible, to keep people from using. Forests, irrigation systems, groundwater basins, grazing land and the atmosphere are others. The key is two properties met earlier. Such resources are nonexcludable like public goods, yet highly rival, because what one user takes is no longer there for others. So they get crowded or overused and suffer big multilateral negative externality problems. River water that anyone nearby can draw, and swordfish that anyone with a boat and gear can catch, are examples. So is old-growth timber in a developing country, where slow regrowth means each cut reduces what is left for others. Ownership varies. Governments may own them as public goods, communities as common property, individuals and firms as private goods. When no one owns them they are open access. {{ref:nature-hist-039}} found many run by local self-managing communities, contradicting the claim that they must be privatized or be destroyed. In James Bay, Quebec, beaver numbers recovered after Indigenous communities' customary hunting laws were legally recognized and outside trappers were banned.

nature-econ-623.title: Ownership and the hold-up problem: who should own the assets
nature-econ-623.text: Grossman, Hart and Moore built an approach that explains firm boundaries through ownership of assets when contracts are incomplete, unable to spell out every future case. Its seminal works, Grossman and Hart (1986), Hart and Moore (1990) and Hart (1995), built the incomplete contracting paradigm. The logic runs through the hold-up problem. Since deals will be renegotiated, each party expects only part of the return on its investment, and so invests too little. It explains the pros and cons of merging firms, and has been applied to providing shared goods and to moving state-owned assets into private hands.

nature-econ-660.title: Public bads: harms no one can escape
nature-econ-660.text: Air pollution reaches everyone downwind, and no one can opt out. A public bad is the mirror image of a public good: something harmful that no one can avoid and that harms everyone at once. Markets supply too little of a public good but too much of a public bad, because those causing it ignore the harm to others. Much of environmental economics is about externalities, or 'public bads'. Deforestation, excess water use and {{ref:nature-hist-084}} use can all be seen as public bads that push harm onto present and future generations. One way to reduce a public bad is for a third party, usually the state, to step in. Green economists suggest judging such impacts as far ahead as the seventh generation.

nature-econ-666.title: Social traps: short-term gain, long-term loss
nature-econ-666.text: Taking the car instead of public transport buys comfort now and more heat-trapping gas released later. That is a social trap: people act for short-term personal gain in a way that, in the long run, leaves the whole group worse off. John Platt introduced the term in a 1973 paper, applying behavioral psychology to Hardin's tragedy of the commons. Social traps are blamed for taking too many fish, {{ref:nature-eco-761}} in the Sahel, rainforest destruction and, above all, climate change. Platt proposed ways out: rewards for green behavior, and penalties such as pollution taxes.

nature-econ-672.title: Four ways to run an auction
nature-econ-672.text: Auctions set prices in a few main ways. In an English auction, bidders openly outbid one another, each bid higher than the last. In a Dutch auction, the auctioneer starts high and lowers the price until someone accepts it or the seller's minimum is reached. In a first-price sealed-bid auction, everyone submits one secret bid at the same time, and the highest bidder pays what they bid. A Vickrey, or second-price sealed-bid, auction works the same way, except that the winner pays the second-highest bid. It is central to {{ref:nature-pol-316}} and to online ad bidding.

nature-econ-741.title: Axelrod's tournaments: how nice strategies won
nature-econ-741.text: Robert Axelrod organized computer tournaments in which strategies submitted by academics competed in the repeated prisoner's dilemma. Greedy strategies did poorly over the long run, and the simple tit for tat won. Axelrod concluded that successful strategies are nice, retaliating, forgiving and non-envious. He used the results to show how altruism could evolve by {{ref:nature-eco-745}} from purely selfish beginnings, reported in his 1984 book The Evolution of Cooperation.

nature-econ-745.title: Discounting: paying to put off a payment
nature-econ-745.text: Most people prefer money now to money later, because of mortality, impatience and salience effects, the pull of what is vivid and close at hand. Discounting builds that preference into a deal. Someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time. The discount is the gap between what is owed today and the larger amount that must be paid later to settle what is owed. Why should a delay cost anything? A payment made in the future is worth less than the same payment today, because money in hand now could be banked to earn interest. The debtor who delays is in effect compensating the creditor for what the money could have earned meanwhile. Most models assume the discount yield equals the return the money could earn elsewhere, at similar risk, over the same period. Discounting also runs the other way, turning a future payment into its present value, also called its discounted value. Either way it rests on the time value of money: the same payment is worth one amount in the future and another today.

nature-econ-802.title: Climateflation: when a warming climate raises prices
nature-econ-802.text: Heat, droughts and flooding hit farm output, and shoppers feel it at the checkout. Climateflation is inflation driven by {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, through its effects on food production and the networks that deliver goods. Isabel Schnabel of the European Central Bank first used the term. In 2022–2023, climate-driven heat in Europe raised food prices by about 0.7%, adding about 0.3% to overall inflation. The same study found that warming expected by 2035 could raise these effects by 30–50%. A related term, {{ref:nature-gov-234}}, describes inflation caused by fossil fuel prices, which push up transport, food and shipping costs.

nature-econ-870.title: The business cycle: booms, busts and their rhythms
nature-econ-870.text: Economies do not grow smoothly. The business cycle is intervals of general expansion followed by recession. The simplest definition calls a recession two consecutive quarters of negative growth in {{ref:nature-econ-483}}; better ones use more indicators, such as consumer confidence, retail trade, unemployment and production indexes. Burns and Mitchell's 1946 standard definition stresses that the fluctuations are widely diffused across the economy. Sismondi's 1819 work was the first systematic account of crises. {{ref:nature-hist-012}} had denied cycles, blamed external factors such as war, or studied only the long term. Juglar first identified cycles of 7 to 11 years in 1860, and later work found Kondratiev waves in world GDP and Kuznets cycles of about 17 years. Commodity price shocks are considered a significant driver of the US cycle, and a majority of post-war recessions are linked to oil price rises. Since the 1940s most developed-nation governments have treated softening the cycle as their responsibility under {{ref:nature-econ-554}}.

nature-econ-871.title: Why economies swing: the business cycle theories
nature-econ-871.text: Economists disagree whether business cycle fluctuations are exogenous or endogenous, that is, whether they come from outside the economy or from within it. The classical school favors outside causes and the Keynesian school inside ones. Mainstream economics sees cycles as the random summation of random causes. Slutzky's 1927 observation that summed random numbers mimic cycles led some to treat cyclicality as an artefact. Keynesian theory says fluctuations in {{ref:nature-econ-868}} settle the economy in short-run equilibrium away from full-employment output, though Keynesian models do not necessarily imply periodic cycles. Real business cycle theory, linked to Kydland and Prescott, attributes fluctuations to random changes in total factor productivity, not monetary shocks. Other schools blame credit. Irving Fisher's account of loan-driven deflation holds that net credit expansion drives booms and bursting bubbles cause depressions. Austrian economists blame excessive bank credit, worsened by too-low central-bank rates, for a boom whose malinvestments are liquidated in the bust. Marxian theory holds that commodity production is intrinsically crisis-prone because profitability tends to fall. Kalecki's political business cycle ties cycles to resistance to sustained full employment.

nature-econ-873.title: The Lorenz curve: drawing inequality
nature-econ-873.text: Line up everyone in a country from poorest to richest, then ask how much income the bottom half holds. The Lorenz curve answers for every share at once. Max Lorenz developed it in 1905, with population share on the x-axis and income share on the y-axis. It graphs the distribution of income or wealth, as in {{ref:nature-econ-494}}. Perfect equality is the line y = x; perfect inequality, where one person has everything, is y = 0 until x = 100%. The curve runs from (0,0) to (1,1) and cannot rise above the equality line. A curve that never lies below another dominates it. The Gini coefficient is the area between the equality line and the curve divided by the area between the equality and inequality lines. Higher means more unequal. The same device describes inequality in {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} and biodiversity studies, plotting the cumulative proportion of species against individuals.

nature-eecon-202.title: Population growth: from one billion to eight
nature-eecon-202.text: In 1800 the world held 1 billion people. By 2026 it held 8.3 billion, and it still adds about 70 million people, or 0.84%, every year. Population growth is simply the increase in the number of people in a {{ref:nature-eco-374}}. Better farming, sanitation and medicine drove the rise. The global growth rate peaked at 2.2% a year in 1963 and has fallen ever since. In rich countries the shift to smaller families, known as the {{ref:nature-eecon-250}}, has slowed growth sharply. Where it ends is uncertain. As of 2024 the UN projects a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s. The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation expects an earlier peak, 9.73 billion in 2064, falling to 8.89 billion by 2100. The environmental stakes are high. Together with rising consumption, population growth drives biodiversity loss and climate change through overuse of natural resources. Reducing population is discussed as a sustainability strategy, but respect for free life choices limits what it can achieve.

nature-eecon-231.title: Waste: what the holder no longer wants
nature-eecon-231.text: Waste is unwanted or unusable material, any substance discarded after primary use or judged worthless or defective. What counts as waste varies by viewer. The EU defines it as an object the holder discards, intends to discard or is required to discard. A by-product is a joint product of minor economic value, and an invention that raises a waste product's value above zero can turn it into a by-product, joint product or resource. Waste is mostly measured by size or weight, which differ: wet organic waste is much heavier, and bottles of equal size can weigh differently. Managing it is costly for municipalities. Pay-as-you-throw policies can cut cost and quantity, and recovery avoids raw material extraction and often cuts transport costs. It is also an {{ref:nature-gov-168}} issue, since burdens fall more often on marginalized groups and residents of developing nations.

nature-eecon-237.title: Waste minimisation: the cheapest waste is never made
nature-eecon-237.text: The cheapest way to manage waste is often not to create it. Waste minimisation is a set of processes and practices meant to reduce the amount of waste produced. It means redesigning products and processes, or changing consumption patterns, rather than treating waste after it arises. The benefits are practical. Firms get more output per unit of raw material, lower purchasing costs, a better reputation and easier compliance with environmental regulation. Scrap can be fed back to the start of the line, and one process's waste can become another's raw material. Waste exchanges cut disposal volumes. Reducing waste in one stage, though, may create it in another. Eliminating overpackaging is an example of {{ref:nature-eecon-023}}. The EU's packaging targets require plastic packaging cuts of 5% by 2030, 10% by 2035 and 15% by 2040. Personal waste reduction is a small part of total waste, but householders can still influence policy. One study suggests a bag tax motivates reuse more than a discount does.

nature-eecon-239.title: Renewable energy: power replenished on a human timescale
nature-eecon-239.text: Renewable energy is made from natural resources replenished on a human timescale. The most widely used types are solar, wind, bioenergy and hydropower, and the IEA defines it as energy from natural processes replenished faster than they are consumed. Replacing fossil fuels with low-emission sources is central to net zero. Renewables are also more evenly spread worldwide than fossil fuels and cut air pollution. The resource is vast. The technical potential of utility-scale solar PV, concentrated solar, onshore wind and offshore wind each exceeds 100 PWh per year, against global energy use of about 65 PWh in 2019. IRENA states that about 86% (187 GW) of renewable capacity added in 2022 cost less than fossil-fuel electricity, and its finance report shows US$499 billion invested that year. Investment in renewables, especially solar, tends to create more jobs than coal, gas or oil. There are catches. Solar and wind are intermittent, with lower capacity factors, while fossil, nuclear and hydropower plants can match the grid's demand. Storage returns energy when production falls below consumption. Critics note that renewables need more metals and minerals whose extraction can cause {{ref:nature-gov-202}}, and installations increasingly threaten conservation areas. Whether nuclear power counts as renewable is debated; legal definitions usually exclude it, with Utah an exception.

nature-eecon-247.title: Urban metabolism: the city as a flow of materials
nature-eecon-247.text: Abel Wolman coined the term in 1965 by modelling the inflows and outflows of a hypothetical American city of 1 million people, mainly water and the waste it produces. Urban metabolism is now a model for describing the flows of materials and energy through cities, as in a city-level {{ref:nature-eecon-019}}. Herbert Girardet contrasted circular metabolism, where nearly everything is reused, with the linear metabolism of cities, with clear resource inputs and waste outputs. The energy method of {{ref:nature-hist-063}} coined {{ref:nature-eecon-099}}, which measures the solar energy used directly or indirectly to make a product, in solar equivalent joules. Tracking materials became the mainstream school because its units are more practical for the public, officials and researchers. Planners use it for four things: {{ref:nature-gov-102}}, urban greenhouse gas accounting, mathematical modelling for policy analysis and urban design.

nature-eecon-249.title: Consumerism: when buying becomes identity
nature-eecon-249.text: Around 1900 the average worker still spent 80-90% of income on food and necessities. Consumerism is the socio-cultural and economic phenomenon in which many people aspire to goods and services beyond what is needed for survival or traditional displays. It emerged in Western Europe and the United States during the Industrial Revolution and became widespread around the 20th century. Buying became cultural, social and identity-forming, not only economic. Mass production and mass consumption, exemplified by Henry Ford, were what was needed to propel it. Critics say consumerist societies damage the environment, contribute to global warming and use resources at a higher rate. Experts link it to the {{ref:nature-eecon-178}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-185}}. Tim Kasser's book argues that people who value wealth and possessions more tend to have lower satisfaction and higher anxiety. Austrian economists object to Keynesian incentives for more consumption, arguing production is what makes consumption possible. Alternatives range from {{ref:nature-eecon-254}} and buying local to freeganism.

nature-eecon-256.title: Robert Solow: growth from technical progress
nature-eecon-256.text: Robert Solow is the American economist behind the Solow-Swan growth model, and he won the 1987 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. His model separates the determinants of growth into increases in inputs (labour and capital) and technical progress. It is called exogenous because the saving rate is taken as given. Using it, Solow (1957) calculated that about four-fifths of the growth in US output per worker came from technical progress. Ecological economics places his strongly neoclassical position, with the position of {{ref:nature-hist-081}}, at one end of a continuum of views on weak versus {{ref:nature-eecon-218}}. Georgescu-Roegen and Daly stand at the other. Solow also criticised Limits to Growth, from {{ref:nature-hist-026}}, as having 'simplistic' scenarios.

nature-es-086.title: Ecosystem engineers: species that build and reshape habitats
nature-es-086.text: Beavers fell trees and build barriers across streams, and in doing so they change the distribution and abundance of many other organisms. They are the original ecosystem engineer: a species that creates, substantially changes, maintains or destroys a habitat. Such species can strongly affect how many species an area holds and how varied its landscape is. They matter because they modify resources, not because they are eaten. Species covered in {{ref:nature-eco-301}} usually matter through feeding relationships instead. By making habitats more varied, beavers can support species not found elsewhere. Conserving one engineer may therefore protect a whole landscape's diversity. Whales release nutrients at the surface that feed phytoplankton and spread them across oceans, the {{ref:nature-eco-365}}. {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} such as kudzu and the zebra mussel often act as engineers. Humans are thought to be the most dramatic engineers of all, through cities, farming, logging, river barriers and mining. Some ecologists see the term as a buzzword, since it may imply intent and every species changes its environment to some degree.

nature-es-092.title: Erosion control: keeping soil in place with plants
nature-es-092.text: New Deal programs in the United States planted 18,000 miles of tree and shrub belts to break the wind, from North Dakota to Texas, to fight soil erosion. Erosion control is the set of practices that prevent or repair soil erosion, chiefly by keeping land covered with plants. Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent erosion by both wind and water. Terracing, cutting slopes into level steps, is a highly effective method practiced for thousands of years around the world. Such belts along fields also improve growing conditions around the crops, shelter birds and store carbon. {{ref:nature-nbs-355}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-276}} and leaving crop residues on the field under {{ref:nature-nbs-291}} all reduce erosion. {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, which mixes crops with trees, works especially well in rainy tropical climates. On coasts, the roots of the trees covered in {{ref:nature-eco-410}} slow water, trap sediment and bind soils. Good erosion control manages surface runoff and helps prevent {{ref:nature-res-261}}, the loss of soil and habitat, and damage to property.

nature-found-005.title: Four kinds of help: sorting ecosystem services
nature-found-005.text: Not every benefit from nature works the same way. Some touch nearby people directly, like fresh water or food. Others act through general conditions, like a steady climate or soil held in place against erosion. To keep track, scientists sort ecosystem services into groups. The best-known scheme, from a United Nations assessment, uses four: regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting. The provisioning group holds the products obtained from ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, wood, fibre and fuel. The regulating group comes from nature keeping its processes in check, through climate control, carbon storage, disease control and control of {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}. The supporting group, such as nutrient cycling and the making of soil, allows the other three to exist; it is the base on which the rest stand. Each group gets its own entry, beginning with {{ref:nature-found-009}}. An ecosystem need not offer all four kinds at once, but people usually benefit from a mix of them. Other schemes redraw the lines. To avoid counting the same benefit twice, a later study, covered in {{ref:nature-hist-001}}, replaced the base layer with habitat services. The Common International Classification for Ecosystem Services keeps the cultural and provisioning groups. It merges regulating and habitat services into one group, {{ref:nature-val-107}} and maintenance services.

nature-found-009.title: Cultural services: beauty, belief and a day outdoors
nature-found-009.text: Some of nature's gifts cannot be eaten or burned. Cultural services are the non-material benefits of nature, such as recreation, beauty, learning and spiritual meaning. They include nature-based tourism and outdoor sports, nature's place in art and national symbols, and its religious or heritage value. They are hard to put a price on. Critics go further, arguing that cultural values attach to unique landscapes and ways of seeing, not to measurable properties of ecosystems. Scholars still disagree over whether such values fit the ecosystem services approach at all.

nature-found-022.title: The biosphere, from 19 km underground to 64 km up
nature-found-022.text: Life turns up at least 19 km underground and at least 64 km up in the atmosphere. It spreads from the polar ice caps to the equator. All of it together makes the biosphere: the sum of all the world's ecosystems, the zone of life on Earth. The biosphere joins every living thing with the rock, ice, water and air around it. For matter, it is almost a closed system, with little arriving or leaving. For {{ref:nature-eecon-238}}, it is open. Living things that capture sunlight do so at around 100 terawatts. Geologist Eduard Suess coined the term in 1875, and Vladimir Vernadsky gave it its ecological meaning in the 1920s. Earth's biosphere is divided into large regions of similar life, and most of the richest lie near the equator.

nature-found-023.title: Environmental degradation: 70% of the land, already altered
nature-found-023.text: Since farming began over 11,000 years ago, people have altered about 70% of Earth's land surface. Along the way they have halved the global mass of vegetation. A 2021 study found that just 3% of Earth's land is still ecologically and faunally intact, with its ecosystems and animal life whole. This is environmental degradation: the worsening of the environment through lost resources such as clean air, water and soil, destroyed ecosystems and habitats, extinct wildlife, and pollution. A UN disaster-reduction body puts it more briefly, as a cut in the environment's capacity to meet social and ecological needs. Degradation runs down the natural capital that ecosystems hold. Some of it is plain to see, like deforestation. Some builds slowly, like plastic pollution, or heat-trapping gases pushing the climate toward tipping points. Its scale depends on more than the number of people. Consumption patterns matter, and so does how efficiently resources are used. Industrialised nations, consuming more per person, often leave a disproportionately large environmental footprint. The harm is not shared evenly either. Women's livelihoods, health, access to food, and access to water and {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} are disproportionately hurt.

nature-found-026.title: Short-termism: the pull of the quick payoff
nature-found-026.text: Some actions take longer than one government's term to show results, and short-termism can undermine them. Short-termism is favouring quick profits and short-term results over long-term results and far-sighted action. It is linked to a thinking habit that prefers short-term payoffs to long-term rewards, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-065}}. Short-termism and {{ref:nature-eecon-249}} are named among the barriers to {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}.

nature-found-036.title: Why externalities happen: ownership and the cost of trading
nature-found-036.text: Land and money are easy to own. Air, water and wild animals cross borders freely, so people use them without paying the full cost. One view holds that externalities come mainly from such poorly defined ownership rights, and from the costs of making deals. A person who gets a flu shot cannot own a share of the herd immunity it creates, so may skip it. The costs of making a deal also block some worthwhile exchanges; without them, people could bargain away every externality. The source itself flags this account as one-sided, calling it a narrow libertarian reading of Coase.

nature-found-044.title: Economics: the science of running the world's household
nature-found-044.text: The word comes from the Ancient Greek oikonomia, the way to run a household. Economics is the social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used. It looks at how economic agents, such as households, firms, buyers and sellers, behave and interact, and how whole economies work. The field was once called {{ref:nature-gov-242}}. Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, is described as the birth of economics as a separate discipline. Smith named land, labour and capital as the basic inputs of production, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-086}}. A widely accepted definition came from Lionel Robbins in 1932. He called economics the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses. Economists divide their field in two ways. One split is by scale: the study of individual agents and markets, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-134}}, versus the study of whole economies, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-541}}. The second includes growth, inflation and unemployment. The other separates positive economics, which describes what is, from normative economics, which argues for what ought to be. Controlled experiments are hard in economics, so theories are mostly tested on observed data, using statistical methods called econometrics. Economic analysis now reaches far beyond business, into law, politics and the environment.

nature-found-050.title: Does market failure even exist
nature-found-050.text: Not every economist accepts the idea of market failure. Arguments from several schools of thought call it misleading, too narrow, or no justification for government action. Some, such as Milton Friedman, argue that government failure may cost more than the market failure it tries to fix. Some Austrian School economists go further and deny that market failure exists. Entrepreneurs seeking profit, they say, remove inefficiencies on their own. Marxian economists take the opposite line: inefficient outcomes are built into {{ref:nature-econ-848}}, not rare exceptions. Inequality raises a different issue. High inequality is often called a market failure in everyday speech. Mainstream economics does not count it as one, because it is not Pareto inefficient: it can exist even when no one could gain without someone else losing. Zerbe and McCurdy add a final twist. Once the costs of making a deal are counted, market failure describes a situation that exists everywhere. The schools still disagree about whether market failure exists and whether it justifies government intervention.

nature-found-064.title: Government failure: when the fix falls short
nature-found-064.text: Government action meant to fix a market failure can itself fall short. Government failure is the economic waste that results, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative. It happens when an intervention's costs outweigh its benefits, leaving society worse off than under another policy or none. It is about inefficiency, not about who wins and loses; simply creating winners and losers is not a government failure. Any form of intervention can fail: provision, taxes or subsidies, and {{ref:nature-val-107}}. Common mechanisms include regulators coming to serve the industries they oversee, {{ref:nature-eco-740}}, and inefficient outcomes that are easier politically than better ones. A small, well-organized interest group, for instance, can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole. The phrase became a term of art in the early 1960s. Coase used it in 1964, warning that all real social arrangements are more or less failures. Some economists argue that government failure can be worse than the market failure it targets.

nature-gov-041.title: SDG 13: climate action
nature-gov-041.text: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, nations agreed to keep warming well under 2 °C. Their pledges would still lead to about 2.7 °C by 2100. Sustainable Development Goal 13, "Climate action," calls for urgent action to limit climate change and adapt to its impacts. Its five targets for 2030 include making societies more resilient to climate disasters and building climate measures into national policy. Target 13.a refers to developed countries' promise to mobilize $100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries. One indicator simply counts the countries with national climate pledges and adaptation plans. COVID-19 cut 2020 emissions about 6% below projections, but the fall was only temporary. Critics say the goal overlooks {{ref:nature-gov-238}} as a way people adapt.

nature-gov-197.title: Conservation refugees
nature-gov-197.text: In Guinea, 663,000 people have been displaced from protected areas. Liberia claims over 120,000 conservation refugees, and Senegal has 65,000 displaced. A conservation refugee is a person, usually Indigenous, pushed from their homeland when a park or reserve is created. Many were already marginalized. They end up on the edges of towns with few opportunities and rarely have legal recourse. The idea behind it is old. The view of {{ref:nature-hist-083}} that wilderness should be emptied of inhabitants became US policy with the 1964 Wilderness Act. The anthropologist Darrell Posey disagreed, arguing that landscapes that look natural may have been shaped by Indigenous peoples.

nature-hist-032.title: World Resources Institute: measuring the planet
nature-hist-032.text: The World Resources Institute, a global non-profit research organization founded in 1982, studies sustainable practices for business, finance and governance. Its work centers on food, forests, water, energy, cities and climate. With companies it developed the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, a common standard for measuring emissions. With Google Earth Engine it built {{ref:nature-hist-082}}, which maps forest change from satellite images. In 1990 Anil Agarwal criticized one of its emissions studies as environmental colonialism.

nature-nbs-351.title: Polyculture: many crops in one field
nature-nbs-351.text: Most farm fields today hold one crop, but that was not always so. Polyculture grows more than one crop species together in the same place at the same time, in contrast to {{ref:nature-nbs-082}}. It was traditionally the most prevalent form of agriculture. Farm chemicals made single-crop farming dominant in developed countries from the 1950s. Around 15% to 20% of the world's agriculture is estimated to still rely on traditional polyculture. It raises total yield, stability and {{ref:nature-eecon-191}}, though each crop's own yield is lower, and crops mainly compete for room, light, water and nutrients. Diverse crops reduce pest and disease losses; the disease-diversity hypothesis holds that more plant diversity lowers disease severity. Polyculture can also cut the release of farm chemicals and freshwater eutrophication, and deep-rooted legumes improve soil structure and drainage. There are drawbacks. Mechanized sowing and spraying become difficult, more manual labour is needed, and compatible combinations can be hard to find.

nature-pol-067.title: Waste-to-energy: power from rubbish
nature-pol-067.text: Rubbish can keep the lights on. Waste-to-energy is generating power from municipal waste, by burning it, by capturing landfill gas, or through {{ref:nature-clim-285}} or gasification, which break waste down with heat. Older incinerators emitted many pollutants. New rules and technology changed that. US rules in 1995 and 2000 cut dioxin emissions from such plants by over 99% below 1990 levels, and mercury by over 90%. Because waste contains food, wood and paper, burning it can partly count as {{ref:nature-res-258}}, energy made from living material.

nature-pol-160.title: Shoot, shovel and shut up: when protection backfires
nature-pol-160.text: In the American West, a grim saying sums up the worst case: 'shoot, shovel, and shut up'. The problem behind it is a {{ref:nature-pol-314}}. Strict species-protection rules can turn an endangered species into a financial burden for the landowner who hosts it. That tempts owners to destroy habitat before the species arrives. Because species could be listed under the {{ref:nature-pol-159}} without considering economic costs, the law soon became controversial. Landowners and industries face lost opportunities and delays. The evidence is more than anecdote. A 1995 study of about 1,000 private forest plots found owners more likely to harvest pines as the trees matured enough to attract endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers. Economists suggest a fix: compensate property owners for protecting species, so a listed species is no longer a potential financial loss. Cooperation can work. Agreements between landowners and the agency helped the woodpecker move from endangered to threatened by 2024. The wider argument goes on. Many hold that the protections curtail economic activity and create such incentives, while others defend the law's species-first approach.

nature-pol-211.title: Forest certification: a label for responsibly managed wood
nature-pol-211.text: About 10% of the world's forest is under at least one certification program. Forest certification is a voluntary system that certifies wood and paper products as coming from forests managed responsibly under a particular standard. An independent body writes the standard, and independent auditors certify forest operations that meet it. Credible programs protect biodiversity and water quality, keep harvests sustainable and require prompt replanting. The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), a collaboration of environmental groups, forest companies and social interests, pioneered third-party certification in the early 1990s. With no single international standard, more than 50 scheme owners now offer certification. The two largest are the FSC and the PEFC, which covers about two-thirds of certified forest area. Critics such as Greenpeace and Jared Diamond question the rigor of rival standards, which some say logging companies set up to confuse consumers. The schemes defend their standards. Demand comes from publishers' paper commitments, green buying by governments, standards for {{ref:nature-eecon-245}} and laws against {{ref:nature-res-139}}.

nature-pol-303.title: Biofuel: fuel grown in a season
nature-pol-303.text: Biofuel is made over a short time span from biomass, rather than by the very slow natural processes that form fossil fuels. It can come from plants or from agricultural, domestic or industrial bio waste, and is mostly used for transport but also for heating and electricity. It is regarded as a {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} source, yet it faces criticism over the food-versus-fuel debate, varied sustainability assessments, and {{ref:nature-eco-053}} and {{ref:nature-eco-035}} from production. Global production was 81 Mtoe in 2017, about 3% a year above 2010. The US led with 37 Mtoe, then Brazil and South America at 23 Mtoe and Europe at 12 Mtoe. Emissions are not inherently carbon-neutral: they depend on feedstock, processing, transport and land-use change, and range from -127.1 gCO2eq per MJ with carbon capture to above 95 gCO2eq per MJ where land-use change is large. EU and UK policies require biofuels to deliver at least 65% greenhouse gas savings against fossil fuels (70% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin). The International Resource Panel concluded that biofuels differ in their effects on climate, the security of energy supply and ecosystems, so effects should be assessed over the whole life cycle.

nature-pol-309.title: Indirect land use change: the emissions biofuels cause elsewhere
nature-pol-309.text: A biofuel can look clean at the field and dirty on the far side of the world. The indirect form of {{ref:nature-res-108}} is the unintended extra carbon emissions from cropland expanding elsewhere to meet global demand for {{ref:nature-pol-303}}. Farmers worldwide respond to higher crop prices by clearing pristine land to replace the food crops diverted to biofuel. Because rainforests and {{ref:nature-eco-467}} store carbon, clearing them raises net greenhouse gas emissions. Some authors argue it also affects biodiversity, water quality, food prices and supply, land tenure, worker migration and community stability. Before 2008, life-cycle studies found corn, cellulosic and Brazilian sugarcane ethanol cut emissions versus gasoline, but none counted these effects. A 2008 Searchinger paper concluded that indirect effects offset the direct gains of corn and cellulosic ethanol. Payback was 4 years for Brazilian sugarcane, 167 for US corn and 52 for cellulosic ethanol, over a 30-year horizon. Critics such as Wang and Haq called the assumptions outdated, and Searchinger replied that ignoring these emissions is wrong however hard they are to predict. The size of the emissions was disputed by the studies' authors and critics. In 2009 the California Air Resources Board included these indirect effects in California's {{ref:nature-pol-165}}, in force in 2011. A 2010 Brazil study projected indirect deforestation of 121,970 km2 by 2020 from sugarcane ethanol and soybean {{ref:nature-pol-305}}, a carbon deficit taking about 250 years to repay.

nature-pol-315.title: The right to know about hazards
nature-pol-315.text: The right to know is the right of people to know about hazards and substances that may harm them, often framed around chemicals. UNESCO defines it as letting people take part in decisions that affect them in an informed way while holding governments and others accountable. In the United States it takes two forms, Community Right to Know and Workplace Right to Know, and appears in the book {{ref:nature-hist-006}} by Rachel Carson. The Bhopal disaster of December 1984, in which a methyl isocyanate cloud killed 2,000 people, drove the push for more hazard information. The Hazard Communication Standard, in force from 1985, makes manufacturers and employers tell workers about chemical hazards, and the 1986 Emergency Planning and Right to Know Act followed.

nature-pol-318.title: Renewable energy certificates in the United States
nature-pol-318.text: A renewable energy certificate is a tradable, non-tangible certificate proving that one megawatt-hour of electricity came from an eligible renewable source and was fed into the grid. Compliance markets arise from renewable portfolio standards in 29 states, DC and Puerto Rico, where utilities buy certificates to prove they supply the required share. Voluntary markets serve customers who choose renewable power. Prices vary with vintage year, location, supply and demand, compliance use and power type. Spot prices for solar certificates generally fell from 2010 to 2014; in New Jersey one went from $665.04 in July 2010 to about $160 in May 2014. The US has no national registry. Regional registries and Green-e audits aim to prevent double counting, though critics say it still lets two parties claim one credit. The idea of {{ref:nature-mkt-144}} is that a purchase brings new renewable energy beyond business as usual; critics call it a subsidy.

nature-pol-321.title: Tariffs: taxes on imports
nature-pol-321.text: From 1790 to 1860, import duties made up about 90% of US federal receipts. A tariff is a duty imposed by a national government or union on imported goods, paid by the importer. Besides raising revenue, it regulates foreign trade by burdening foreign products to encourage or safeguard domestic industry. Douglas Irwin says tariffs have served three purposes: revenue, protection of domestic producers, and securing reciprocity through trade agreements. Protective tariffs are among the most widely used tools of {{ref:nature-res-270}}, along with import and export quotas and other non-tariff barriers. Economic analyses generally find that tariffs distort the free market and raise prices of both foreign and domestic products. Welfare effects on the importing country are usually negative even without retaliation. The 1930 Smoot-Hawley act raised the average tariff on dutiable imports from about 40% to 47%. Duty is often charged ad valorem on a transaction value, with goods identified by Harmonized System codes developed by the World Customs Organization.

nature-res-220.title: Exploiting natural resources to fuel growth
nature-res-220.text: In the 19th century, mining, steam power and machinery pushed extraction far beyond pre-industrial levels. The exploitation of natural resources means using them, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development. Two forces speed it up: better technology, which makes extraction faster, and rising consumption and {{ref:nature-eecon-249}}, which raise demand. The costs often land on others. Exploitation tends to bring environmental damage, human insecurity and social conflict. Foreign industries often take raw materials from developing countries, and local communities see little of the profit. Soil shows the scale. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) finds that about 33% of the Earth's soils are moderately to highly degraded, and that more than 90% could be by 2050. The rule for sustainable use is simple to state: consume a resource no faster than it is supplied. Not everyone accepts that resources are finite at all. The economist Julian Simon argued that substitution, {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} and new technology make scarcity ever more doubtful, a view others strongly dispute.

nature-val-112.title: Ecological modernization: can markets and states fix the environment?
nature-val-112.text: Can the economy be greened without being slowed? Ecological modernization is a school of thought arguing that the state and the market can work together to protect the environment. It emerged in the early 1980s among scholars at Free University and the Social Science Research Centre in Berlin, including Joseph Huber, Martin Jänicke and Udo Simonis. Its basic assumption is that economy and nature can be combined: productive use of natural resources and environmental media can be a source of growth, like labour and capital productivity. Its tools include energy efficiency and {{ref:nature-eecon-191}}, clean technologies, environmental management, substitution of hazardous substances and product design for environment, with radical innovations changing industrial metabolism. It also draws on {{ref:nature-eecon-017}}, {{ref:nature-acct-050}} of products, and 'cradle to cradle' manufacturing as against 'cradle to grave'. Scholars differ on whether it is only techno-industrial policy or includes cultural change, and on whether government, markets or civil society should lead. All expect innovative structural change. Business may favour it because it meets the {{ref:nature-acct-114}} without challenging free-market principles. Many views within the environmental movement see free trade and self-regulation as part of the problem. Critics call it {{ref:nature-nbs-075}} that leaves capitalism's impulses to degrade the environment intact. They say it ignores {{ref:nature-gov-173}}, applies mostly to Germany and the Netherlands, and rests on an impossible 'sustainable growth'. Its effectiveness and applicability remain a contentious area of environmental social science.
